topics.title: Relational databases, ACID and transactions

kcs.statement: A relational database stores data as rows in tables with a fixed schema and links tables through foreign keys, which SQL joins follow at query time.

ACID means atomicity (all of a transaction's writes commit or none do), consistency (constraints hold after every commit), isolation (concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work) and durability (committed data survives a crash).
Multi-row changes that must succeed together, such as debiting one account and crediting another, belong in one transaction so a crash midway leaves neither change applied.

serves.reason: Naming SQL as the store type and justifying it requires knowing what transactions and ACID guarantee

problem_ideas: A money transfer debits A, then the server crashes before crediting B: which ACID letter prevents the lost money?
Two users book the last seat at the same moment: which property decides that only one succeeds?

topics.title: Database indexes and what they cost writes

kcs.statement: A B-tree index on a column turns a lookup by that column from a full table scan, O(n) rows read, into a tree search of about O(log n) page reads.
Every secondary index must be updated on each insert, and on each update to the indexed column, so adding indexes speeds reads but slows writes and uses extra storage.
A composite index on (a, b) serves queries that filter on a, or on a and b, but not queries that filter only on b.

requires.reason: Indexes are defined on table columns; the lesson needs the relational table model

problem_ideas: A 100M-row users table is queried by email 5,000 times a second with no index: estimate rows read per query with and without a B-tree

topics.title: Normalization: store each fact once

kcs.statement: Normalization stores each fact in exactly one row, so an update touches one place and copies cannot disagree (no update anomaly).
A normalized schema answers reads that combine entities with joins, which grow expensive as tables grow and are hard to run when tables live on different machines.

requires.reason: Normalization is defined over relational tables and foreign keys

problem_ideas: An orders table repeats the customer's address on every row; show the update anomaly when the customer moves

topics.title: Denormalization and materialized views

kcs.statement: Denormalization copies data into the rows that read it, such as storing author_name on each post, so a hot read needs no join.
Denormalized copies must be updated on every write to the source, so denormalization suits read-heavy workloads and risks copies drifting out of sync.
A materialized view stores the precomputed result of a query and is refreshed on a schedule or on change, trading freshness for read speed.

requires.reason: Denormalization is defined as deliberately undoing normalization; the lesson needs it as the baseline

problem_ideas: A feed reads 100:1 over writes and joins posts with users on every read: decide what to denormalize

topics.title: NoSQL and the BASE trade-off

kcs.statement: NoSQL is a family of non-relational data models (key-value, document, wide-column, graph); many NoSQL stores trade joins and multi-record transactions for flexible schemas and built-in partitioning, but some offer transactions and strongly consistent reads, so guarantees must be checked per store.

BASE (basically available, soft state, eventually consistent) is an optional design approach that favours answering during failures and letting replicas converge later; it is a choice some stores make, not a property of every NoSQL store nor the opposite of ACID.

serves.reason: Choosing a NoSQL store type requires knowing which guarantees a given store keeps or drops compared with a relational one

requires.reason: BASE is introduced by comparison with ACID transactions

topics.title: Key-value stores

kcs.statement: A key-value store gives efficient lookup and write of a value by its key (exact cost and latency depend on the implementation: hash table, B-tree or LSM-tree) and cannot query by fields inside the value without a separately maintained index.
Key-value stores fit lookups by ID with no relations, such as sessions, shopping carts, short-code-to-URL mappings and feature flags.

serves.reason: Key-value is one of the four store types the outcome asks the learner to name and justify

requires.reason: Key-value stores are introduced as one NoSQL family

topics.title: Document stores

kcs.statement: A document store keeps self-contained JSON-like documents whose fields may differ between documents and can be queried and indexed by fields inside the document.
Document stores fit data read as one aggregate, such as a product with its variants or a user profile, and fit poorly when many-to-many relationships need joins.

serves.reason: Document store is one of the four store types the outcome asks the learner to name and justify

requires.reason: Document stores are introduced as one NoSQL family

topics.title: Wide-column stores

kcs.statement: A wide-column store such as Cassandra or Bigtable groups rows by a partition key and keeps each partition's rows sorted by a clustering key, so range reads within one partition are fast.
Wide-column stores suit very high write volumes with known query shapes, such as chat messages keyed by (conversation_id, timestamp), and need one table per query pattern.

serves.reason: Wide-column is one of the four store types the outcome asks the learner to name and justify

requires.reason: Wide-column stores are introduced as one NoSQL family

topics.title: Graph databases in one idea

kcs.statement: A graph database stores nodes and edges and follows relationships by traversal, so multi-hop queries like friends-of-friends stay fast where SQL would need repeated self-joins.

requires.reason: Graph databases are introduced as one NoSQL family

lens.reason: Rarely the main store in an interview; worth one sentence when a prompt is about relationships.

topics.title: Object storage for files and media

kcs.statement: Object storage (S3-style) keeps immutable blobs under keys in a flat namespace with metadata, accessed over HTTP; it scales cheaply to petabytes but cannot update part of an object in place.
Images and videos go in object storage while the database keeps only each object's key and metadata, and the bytes are served to users through a CDN.

serves.reason: Photo, video and chat case studies in a mock interview all need media stored outside the database

problem_ideas: Instagram stores 100M photos a day at 2 MB each: compute yearly storage and say where it lives

topics.title: Choosing SQL or NoSQL for a workload

kcs.statement: Choose a relational database when the data is relational and you need joins, multi-row transactions or strict constraints, as with orders and payments; relational databases can also scale out with read replicas and sharding.

Choose a specific NoSQL store by comparing it on access pattern (lookup by a known key, whole-aggregate reads, partition-plus-range reads), schema flexibility, transaction scope, consistency options and built-in partitioning, not on the belief that only NoSQL scales.
A design may use several stores, each matched to one access pattern, for example SQL for orders, a key-value store for sessions and object storage for images.

serves.reason: The outcome's product is a named store type with a stated trade-off; this topic is that decision

requires.reason: The SQL side of the choice rests on transactions and joins
The NoSQL side of the choice rests on which guarantees a given store keeps or drops

topics.title: Replication and leader-follower setups

kcs.statement: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several nodes so the data survives a node loss and read load can be spread across copies.
In leader-follower replication all writes go to one leader, which streams its changes to followers that serve reads; read capacity grows with followers but write capacity stays that of one node.
When the leader of a leader-follower setup dies, writes stop until a follower is promoted to leader and clients are redirected to it.

serves.reason: The outcome requires naming a replication mode; leader-follower is the default one

topics.title: Synchronous vs asynchronous replication

kcs.statement: With synchronous replication the leader acknowledges a write only after a follower has stored it, so no acknowledged write is lost if the leader dies, but every write pays the follower round trip and stalls if that follower is down.
With asynchronous replication the leader acknowledges a write immediately and ships it to followers afterwards, giving low write latency but losing the not-yet-replicated writes if the leader dies.

serves.reason: The outcome's replication mode must be stated with its trade-off, which is the sync vs async choice

requires.reason: Sync and async describe how the leader ships writes to followers

problem_ideas: A follower in another region is 80 ms away: compute write latency under sync vs async replication

topics.title: Replication lag and read-your-writes

kcs.statement: Replication lag is the delay between a write committing on the leader and appearing on a follower, so a read served by a follower can return stale data.
To give a user read-your-writes, route that user's reads to the leader for a short window after they write, or until the follower has applied that write.

requires.reason: Lag only arises with asynchronous shipping to followers

problem_ideas: A user edits their bio and refreshes 300 ms later; lag is 1 s: predict what they see and fix it
Lag spikes to 30 s during a batch import: list which features break

Pick which reads in a banking app must never go to a follower

lens.reason: A frequent interviewer follow-up after you add read replicas: 'what if the user reads their own write?'

topics.title: Multi-leader replication and write conflicts

kcs.statement: Multi-leader replication lets more than one node accept writes, typically one leader per region, so writes stay local and a region's loss does not stop writes elsewhere.
Two leaders can accept conflicting writes to the same record before they sync, so a multi-leader setup needs a conflict-resolution rule.
Last-write-wins keeps the write with the latest timestamp and silently discards the other, which loses data when writes are concurrent or clocks are skewed.

requires.reason: Multi-leader is taught as the extension of single-leader replication
Conflicts exist because leaders replicate to each other asynchronously

lens.reason: Comes up for multi-region prompts; most designs stay single-leader, so know when not to use it.

topics.title: Strong, eventual and weak consistency

kcs.statement: Under strong consistency every read returns the most recent acknowledged write, which typically requires reading from the leader or waiting for replicas to agree.
Under eventual consistency replicas may return stale values for a while but converge to the same value once new writes stop.
Under weak consistency a read may never see a given write, which is acceptable for data such as live video frames or game positions where only the latest value matters.

serves.reason: The outcome requires stating a consistency level for the chosen store

requires.reason: The models are defined by how they treat lag between replicas

topics.title: CAP theorem: what you give up during a partition

kcs.statement: During a network partition, a replicated store cannot guarantee both linearizable consistency and availability: preserving consistency can require refusing or delaying requests, and preserving availability can require returning responses that may be stale or otherwise violate consistency.
A CP system, such as a bank ledger, rejects requests it cannot confirm during a partition; an AP system, such as a shopping cart or like counter, keeps serving and reconciles afterwards.
A networked store cannot opt out of partitions, so 'CA' is not a real choice for it; when there is no partition the remaining trade-off is latency against consistency.

serves.reason: Justifying the consistency level against availability is the trade-off the outcome asks for

requires.reason: CAP's C is strong consistency; the lesson cannot state the theorem without it

topics.title: Quorum reads and writes: R + W > N

kcs.statement: In leaderless (Dynamo-style) replication a client sends each write and read to several replicas directly, with no single leader ordering writes.
With N replicas, writing to W and reading from R where R + W > N guarantees the read set overlaps the latest write set, so at least one replica read holds the latest value.
Lowering W or R speeds that operation and tolerates more unavailable replicas for it; with N=3, W=1, R=3, writes succeed with one replica up but reads fail if any replica is down.

serves.reason: Stating a tunable consistency level for a leaderless store means choosing N, R and W

requires.reason: Quorum settings are explained by the consistency they buy

topics.title: Partitioning: vertical, horizontal and federation

kcs.statement: Partitioning splits one dataset across nodes so each holds a fraction of the data and serves a fraction of the queries, which raises write capacity where replication alone cannot.
Vertical partitioning splits data by columns or tables, while horizontal partitioning splits the rows of one table by a key value.
Federation splits a database by function, such as separate users, products and orders databases, which cuts per-database load but turns cross-function queries into application-side joins.

serves.reason: Deciding whether and how to split data comes before choosing a shard key

problem_ideas: A 20 TB table on 4 TB nodes: compute the minimum number of horizontal partitions

topics.title: Sharding strategies: range, hash and directory

kcs.statement: Sharding is horizontal partitioning across separate database servers, where each shard owns the rows whose shard key maps to it.

Range sharding keeps adjacent keys together so range scans hit one shard, but sequential keys like timestamps all land on the newest shard; hash sharding spreads keys evenly but sends range scans to every shard.
Directory-based sharding keeps a lookup table from key to shard, which lets individual keys move but adds a lookup per query and a component that must stay available.

serves.reason: The outcome's shard key choice is made within a sharding strategy

requires.reason: Sharding is defined as horizontal partitioning across servers

problem_ideas: Shard orders by created_at range across 8 shards and predict the load on each during today's traffic

topics.title: Choosing a shard key and avoiding hot shards

kcs.statement: A good shard key has high cardinality, spreads load evenly and matches the dominant access pattern so most queries touch a single shard.
A skewed shard key, such as a celebrity's user_id or the current date, sends most traffic to one shard; fixes include salting the key with a suffix or splitting that key's data across shards.
Queries that do not filter on the shard key must scatter to every shard and gather the results, and joins or transactions across shards need application logic.

serves.reason: The outcome's product explicitly includes a justified shard key

requires.reason: Choosing a key presupposes knowing how keys map to shards

topics.title: Consistent hashing

kcs.statement: With hash(key) mod N placement, changing N from 4 to 5 moves about 80% of keys, because a key stays only when both remainders agree.
Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on the same hash ring and assigns each key to the first node clockwise from the key's position.
Adding or removing one node on a hash ring moves only the keys in that node's arc, about 1/N of all keys.
A ring lookup binary-searches the sorted node positions for the first position at or after the key's hash, wrapping to the first position when the hash is past the last one.

serves.reason: Mock deep dives on caches and key-value stores expect consistent hashing to explain adding nodes without mass remapping

requires.reason: Consistent hashing is taught as the fix for hash-based sharding's remapping

topics.title: Virtual nodes and replicas on the ring

kcs.statement: Giving each physical node many virtual nodes (positions on the ring) evens out arc sizes, and lets a larger machine take a bigger share by owning more virtual nodes.
To replicate on a ring, store each key on the next N distinct physical nodes clockwise, skipping virtual nodes that belong to a physical node already chosen.

requires.reason: Virtual nodes extend the hash ring and its lookup

topics.title: Putting it together: a storage design in 5 minutes

kcs.statement: A storage answer names, for each main entity, the store type, replication mode, shard key and consistency level, deriving each from the access pattern, read-to-write ratio and storage estimate.
Each storage choice is stated with one trade-off it accepts, for example 'asynchronous replication: low write latency, may lose the last seconds of writes if the leader fails'.
Shard only when the storage estimate or write QPS exceeds what one replicated leader can hold or absorb; below that, a single leader with read replicas is simpler and keeps joins and transactions.
